title: Advance Athlete Lab Safety, Readiness, and Load Management Policy
license: Owned content — cleared for AI retrieval

chunks.heading: Red flags that stop training and trigger referral
chunks.body: Stop the session and advise professional assessment for: chest pain, pressure, or tightness; fainting, blackouts, or unexplained severe shortness of breath; new neurological symptoms such as numbness, weakness, slurred speech, or one-sided symptoms; sudden severe joint pain, an audible pop with instability, or inability to bear weight; suspected stress fracture (sharp localized bone pain that worsens with impact and is tender to touch); fever or systemic illness; and any pain that wakes the athlete at night or steadily worsens over two weeks. In these cases the coach must not prescribe rehabilitation or a workaround plan — it defers to a clinician.

chunks.heading: Acute:chronic workload ratio in practice
chunks.body: Comparing the last 7 days of load against a rolling 28-day average gives a rough spike detector. Ratios near 0.8-1.3 usually reflect steady progression; sustained values above roughly 1.5 mean the recent week is far heavier than the athlete is conditioned for and warrant flattening or cutting the next week; values below 0.8 for several weeks indicate detraining or a return-to-training situation that should be rebuilt gradually. ACWR is a coarse signal, not a diagnosis: interpret it alongside sleep, soreness, HRV trend, and whether the change was planned. Never increase load on the basis of a low ratio alone if the athlete reports pain.

chunks.heading: Adjusting sessions for poor readiness
chunks.body: When recovery markers are poor — sleep score well below the athlete's norm, HRV flagged as unbalanced or suppressed, resting heart rate elevated several beats above baseline, or high subjective stress — downgrade rather than delete. First step: convert a hard session to easy aerobic at the same duration. Second step: cut duration by roughly a third. Third step, if two or more markers are poor or symptoms include heavy legs and low motivation for multiple days, prescribe rest or mobility only. Do not schedule two consecutive hard days when the previous 48 hours show poor recovery.

chunks.heading: Training around common injuries
chunks.body: General conservative substitutions for athletes with a currently active issue: knee pain — avoid deep loaded knee flexion, plyometrics, and downhill running; favour cycling, swimming, and hip-dominant strength. Lower back pain — avoid loaded spinal flexion and heavy axial loading; favour walking, swimming, anti-extension core work. Achilles or calf issues — avoid speed work, hills, and jumping; favour cycling and controlled isometric calf loading. Shoulder pain — avoid overhead pressing and freestyle swim volume; favour lower-body and scapular strength work. These are risk-reduction defaults for planning, not treatment: an athlete with a painful active injury should be advised to seek assessment.

chunks.heading: Conservative return to training
chunks.body: After illness or injury, restart at roughly half the previous volume with all sessions easy, then progress about 10-20% per week only while the athlete stays pain-free during, immediately after, and the morning after each session. Reintroduce intensity last, after two to three consistent easy weeks. Any return of pain moves the athlete back one week of progression. Following a viral illness with fever, wait until symptom-free for at least 24-48 hours, then add several easy days before any intensity. Never compress this timeline to protect a goal event date; move the goal instead.

chunks.heading: Scope of an AI coach
chunks.body: The coach provides training guidance, not medical, physiotherapy, or nutrition-therapy advice, and must say so when a question approaches those boundaries. It does not diagnose conditions, name a suspected pathology as fact, prescribe medication or supplements for clinical purposes, or design rehabilitation protocols. It does not set aggressive weight-loss targets or restrictive intake plans, and it treats signs of disordered eating or relative energy deficiency as referral topics. When evidence is unclear it says so plainly rather than inventing a citation, and it always leaves the athlete a safe fallback option for the day.

chunks.heading: Medication and NSAIDs are outside coaching
chunks.body: The coach never recommends ibuprofen, other NSAIDs, acetaminophen, or any dose of a painkiller so the athlete can train. Masking pain to complete a session hides tissue load and can worsen injury. Medication, imaging, and diagnosis belong to a licensed clinician. If the athlete asks what to take, the answer is: do not self-prescribe from a training chat; speak to a physician or pharmacist, and treat today as rest or pain-free mobility only.

chunks.heading: When the playbook has no match
chunks.body: If retrieval does not return a high-confidence chunk, the coach must not invent a paper, author, year, or DOI. Say the playbook does not cover that method, give a conservative boundary (what will not be prescribed), and keep the athlete inside existing safety rules. New findings are added only as curated, licensed playbook chunks — not by live-scraping the web into the prompt.

chunks.heading: Pain traffic-light coaching rule
chunks.body: Green: mild awareness that settles during warm-up and does not worsen next day — proceed carefully. Yellow: pain that alters form or rises during the session — stop quality, switch to easy or stop. Red: sharp, radiating, neurological, night pain, or inability to bear weight — stop and refer. Never 'push through' red.

chunks.heading: Return after illness
chunks.body: Fever, chest symptoms, or systemic illness: no hard training. After fever clears, restart easy aerobic and rebuild over several days. Viral myocarditis risk means chest pain, undue breathlessness, or fainting → medical care, not a tough-it-out ride.

chunks.heading: Head injury and concussion boundary
chunks.body: Suspected concussion (head impact, confusion, headache, nausea, balance issues): stop training and seek medical assessment. This coach does not clear return-to-play after head injury.

chunks.heading: Low energy availability warning signs
chunks.body: Persistent fatigue, recurring injury, missed periods, obsession with weight, or declining performance with high volume may signal low energy availability. Refer to qualified clinicians. Never prescribe crash diets or extreme restriction.

chunks.heading: Heat, cold, and storm safety
chunks.body: Extreme heat: shorten, slow, hydrate, prefer shade/early hours. Lightning and severe storms: abort outdoor sessions. Icy roads and black ice: swap to indoor or cancel. Safety beats Strava aesthetics.

chunks.heading: NSAID and painkiller boundary
chunks.body: Do not advise ibuprofen, other NSAIDs, or opioids for training pain. Masking pain can worsen injury. Refer medication questions to a clinician. Training edits first: reduce load, change modality, rest.

chunks.heading: Special populations — refer don't prescribe
chunks.body: Pregnancy, postpartum return, cardiac history, uncontrolled diabetes, eating disorders, and post-surgical rehab require clinician-guided plans. Coach only inside clearance and general healthy-adult patterns.

chunks.heading: Honest symptom reporting
chunks.body: Athletes under-report pain to 'stay on plan'. Invite honesty: better a modified week than a six-week injury. Empathy first, then a concrete easier session — never shame.

chunks.heading: Immediate response to a load spike
chunks.body: If this week jumped hard versus the last month: keep frequency, cut intensity, protect sleep, and delay the next quality session. One easy week repairs more than stubborn grey-zone grinding.

chunks.heading: Youth athletes — extra caution
chunks.body: Growing athletes need more recovery, careful early specialization limits, and medical input for persistent pain. This product focuses on adult coaching; escalate youth medical questions.

chunks.heading: Chest pain — stop and escalate
chunks.body: Chest pain, pressure, or unexplained severe breathlessness during exercise: stop, escalate to emergency/medical care, do not continue a 'cool-down test'. Coach sets escalate true and refuses workaround intensity.

chunks.heading: Neurological red flags
chunks.body: Numbness, weakness, slurred speech, one-sided symptoms, or saddle anesthesia: stop training and seek urgent care. No training plan substitutes for assessment.

chunks.heading: Shared decision-making after injury
chunks.body: After minor niggles, offer options: modality swap, shorter easy, or rest day. Let the athlete choose within safe bounds. Document the choice in the plan so the calendar matches.

chunks.heading: Gradual exposure after fear of pain
chunks.body: Athletes returning from pain may fear movement. Use graded easy exposure within clinician guidance. Celebrate completion of easy sessions. Do not force breakthrough workouts to 'prove' readiness.
